assessment.nobel_worthiness: The collateral-constraint mechanism for credit cycles gave macroeconomics a tractable account of how small shocks are amplified and persist. It underlies much later work on financial frictions and crisis dynamics, and it speaks directly to questions that policy has had to face since 2008.
assessment.attribution: The core mechanism comes from Kiyotaki and Moore's 1997 paper on credit cycles. Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the adjacent financial-accelerator and empirical-transmission branch, which overlaps with the Bernanke-Gertler line already recognised in 2022. A prize for the foundational mechanism would therefore centre on the two.
assessment.maturity: Nearly three decades of citations, extensions, quantitative models and policy use. The idea is well established and has held up through repeated crises.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with the 2022 recognition of banking and financial-crisis work.
Whether the committee would prefer a broader macro-finance prize that includes Gertler or Gilchrist.
The mechanism is theory-led, and the case for empirical validation is less direct.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This body of work changed how economists and policymakers understand the labour-market effects of technology and trade. It documents task-based change, job polarisation and the local labour-market costs of import competition, and it has had very large influence on academic and policy debate.
assessment.attribution: Autor's role is central across the task framework and the China-shock work. Hanson is key to the trade-shock research. Katz is central to the earlier skill-biased technical change literature but is also credited under another ballot item. Dorn is a core co-author of the China-shock papers but more junior.
assessment.maturity: The core papers date from the early 2000s through the 2010s and have been tested extensively. Some interpretation of the China shock is still contested, including magnitude, persistence and mechanism.
uncertainties: How to weigh Katz's earlier skill-premium work against the China-shock work when choosing among Katz, Dorn and others.
Ongoing debate about the size and persistence of the trade-shock effects.
The task-based model draws on contributions beyond the credited names, for example Acemoglu.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The heterogeneous-firm model of trade opened a new paradigm after the 2008 prize for new trade theory. It explains selection, within-industry reallocation and the gains from trade, and it became the workhorse of modern trade research.
assessment.attribution: Melitz's 2003 model is the clear core contribution. Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple on exports versus FDI, and his broader theory contributions, add to the case. Redding's role is more about later quantitative and spatial extensions. Helpman also appears in a separate political-economy trade ballot item.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of use, with heavy empirical validation and extensions.
uncertainties: Whether Krugman's 2008 prize reduces the appetite for another trade-theory award.
The balance between the Melitz model and the quantitative or empirical trade literature that followed it, which is credited under other ballot items.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation framework provided a quantitative way to link firm-level distortions to aggregate productivity and cross-country income gaps. It is influential in growth, development and macro-productivity research.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow's 2009 paper is the central contribution. Restuccia's related work with Rogerson on policy distortions is also important, but Rogerson is not among the credited names, so a laureate set including Restuccia alone would be incomplete.
assessment.maturity: About fifteen years of substantial replication and extension, with measurement debates still active.
uncertainties: Concerns that measured dispersion in revenue productivity may reflect measurement error or adjustment costs rather than true misallocation.
The attribution problem created by the omission of Rogerson from the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bayesian persuasion and information design extend the mechanism-design and information-economics tradition to the choice of information structures. They have applications in communication, regulation, platforms and auctions, and they connect to recent prizes for auction and contract theory.
assessment.attribution: Kamenica and Gentzkow introduced Bayesian persuasion. Bergemann and Morris developed the general information-design and robust-predictions framework. Choosing three of the four is hard, and Gentzkow is also known for separate empirical work on media.
assessment.maturity: The core work dates from 2011 and later, so it is younger than the other leading candidates. Empirical applications are still limited relative to the theory.
uncertainties: Attribution among four strong contributors, and whether the field is mature enough.
The balance between theoretical influence and empirical or policy use.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data gave credible measurement of intergenerational mobility and of neighbourhood effects. The work has had a large influence on public policy and on how empirical economists use linked tax and census records.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the central figure. Hendren is key on neighbourhood exposure effects, and Friedman and Katz are important co-authors. The collaborative team structure complicates attribution.
assessment.maturity: The core results are from the 2014 and later period. Replication and long-run validation are still under way.
uncertainties: Some findings depend on proprietary or restricted data, which limits independent replication.
Whether the impact is mature enough, and how to divide credit among a large team.
Chetty also appears under the optimal-taxation ballot item.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rigorous empirical tests and quantification of adverse selection and moral hazard in insurance markets connect classic information theory to data and policy. They inform the design of health insurance and risk-adjustment systems.
assessment.attribution: Finkelstein and Einav are leaders of the empirical selection-market literature, and Salanie contributed testing methods and theory (Chiappori and Salanie). Chiappori is also credited on another ballot item.
assessment.maturity: Two decades of development. Methods are well established, and the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment adds experimental evidence.
uncertainties: Whether the field is seen as a new discovery or an application of the Akerlof-Stiglitz-Rothschild tradition already recognised.
The difficulty of limiting the prize to a small set of names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Formal models of fairness and reciprocity explain systematic departures from selfish behaviour in experiments. They changed how economists model preferences and incentives. Many of the core experimental patterns have been reproduced across large replication efforts and cultures.
assessment.attribution: The Fehr-Schmidt inequity-aversion model and the Fehr-Gachter evidence on reciprocity are central. Falk's role is in later field and survey extensions. Rabin's fairness theory, which is adjacent but not credited here, complicates the exact credit.
assessment.maturity: About 25 years of testing. The qualitative findings are robust, but external validity and the best model specification are still debated.
uncertainties: Debate over how well lab-based social-preference measures predict behaviour in the field.
Competing models and the contribution of Rabin and others outside this ballot item.
I work in an adjacent area (experimental and behavioural economics), so I flag this ranking as a potential conflict and have applied the same criteria as for other fields.
